## Summary

Research confidence is **Moderate**. Some of this break's ideal conditions are confirmed by sources; others rest on limited evidence. It is the class the app computes from the evidence (how well the break's ideal conditions are documented), not a forecast and not a probability.

Main gaps:

- Limited information is available about the wave sizes this break works in.
- This break has no listed tide preference to compare the sources with.
- Limited information is available about the swell period this break needs.
- No survey, scientific or official source confirms the best swell direction.

Research notes (research_evidence.json):

> Eight publishers: seven read directly (Wikipedia, Surf-Forecast, The Inertia, WannaSurf, ABC News, The Age, Surf Atlas) and Surfer Today (two 403 pages) kept as web_search. Wind is consistent: N offshore (Surf-Forecast) and NNE (Wikipedia), both within 15 deg of the profile's 10. Swell direction: SSW and SW (Surf-Forecast) and huge SW (WannaSurf) fit the profile's 200-225. Wikipedia's WSW is 22.5 deg past the optimum (agrees false). Tide (profile null): Wikipedia says medium to high; Surf-Forecast says best around high tide. WannaSurf's 'Low tide only' comes from a page that mixes two spots and was not used. The evidence leans to mid_to_high or high. Season: winter or June-August from three publishers. Size is still the weak variable. No readable source gives a face-height working range. Wikipedia says 1 m+ (scale unclear) and Surf Atlas says 1 m+ on the swell charts, best at 2 m+. Neither can be compared with the profile's 8-40 ft. Surf Atlas mentions regular 20-30 ft walls (recorded under bathymetry and shape, not as a range). Surfnerd's 4-25 ft range is behind a 403 and was not used. Period: none. No readable source gives a number, and forecast periods are excluded. Bathymetry is qualitative: a shallow ledge or shelf of sharp rock reef, boulders on the bottom and in front of the face, the steps. No survey or peer-reviewed source exists; Crossref found nothing for Shipstern. Parks Tasmania's linked page did not respond. In the resume pass, the remaining Wikipedia references were checked: the Red Bull page returned no text, the SMH 2005 article mentions Shipstern only in passing, and news.com.au did not respond. Yeeew lists no Tasmanian spots. Several of the sources are news features (ABC 2015, The Age 2006). They are dated but anecdotal and support only bathymetry and shape.

## Ideal conditions

Directions are compass degrees the swell or wind comes FROM, ranges clockwise. Heights keep the scale each source states (breaking face, Hawaiian, swell or relative to the surfer); the app's sizes are breaking face heights in feet. Sources are numbered as in [Sources](#sources).

### Swell height

| Field | Research value | Status | Sources | App model setting |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Minimum suitable | 1 m; converted: 3.3 ft; open ended above: yes (swell chart height per Surf Atlas; scale not stated by Wikipedia) | documented | S1, S9 | `wave_height_min_ft` 8 ft (breaking face) |
| Ideal range | 2 m or more; converted: 6.6 ft or more (swell chart height) | documented | S9 | no separate setting; working range 8–40 ft |
| Maximum suitable | — | not documented | — | `wave_height_max_ft` 40 ft (breaking face) |

Notes:

- **Minimum suitable**: Surf Atlas says it needs at least a metre on the swell charts (offshore swell, not breaking faces) to get going and Wikipedia that it holds and breaks from 1 metre plus in winter without stating the scale; 1 m is about 3.3 ft (1 / 0.3048).
  - S9 (Surf Atlas (thesurfatlas.com)): “The spot needs at least a meter in the swell charts to get going, and really hits its finest when its at least double that.”
  - S1 (Wikipedia): “It is known to hold and break from 1 metre plus in winter.”
- **Ideal range**: Surf Atlas says it really hits its finest at at least double its 1 m swell-chart minimum, i.e. 2 m or more of offshore swell (about 6.6 ft by 2 / 0.3048); no upper bound is given.
  - S9 (Surf Atlas (thesurfatlas.com)): “The spot needs at least a meter in the swell charts to get going, and really hits its finest when its at least double that.”
- **Maximum suitable**: No excerpt states the largest size it holds; Surf Atlas's regular 20-30 foot walls and The Age's 20-foot face describe waves seen there, not a limit.

### Swell direction

| Field | Research value | Status | Sources | App model setting |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ideal bearing | 202.5° (SSW) [S2] · 225° (SW) [S6] · 247.5° (WSW) [S1] | conflicting | S1, S2, S6 | `optimal_swell_direction` 200–225° (SSW to SW, clockwise) |
| Acceptable range | — | not documented | — | `swell_window` 180–250° (S to WSW, clockwise) |
| Blocked directions | — | not documented | — | no separate setting (outside `swell_window`) |
| Exposure | exposed reef break with quite reliable surf; swells arrive out of the deep Southern Ocean | documented | S2, S5 | no setting |

Notes:

- **Ideal bearing**: Surf-Forecast gives south southwest (202.5 deg) as the best swell direction, WannaSurf says it breaks best on a huge SW swell (225 deg) and Wikipedia lists WSW (247.5 deg), so the three best directions span 45 deg.
  - S2 (Surf-Forecast.com): “Most of the surf here comes from groundswells and the best swell direction is from the south southwest.”
  - S6 (WannaSurf): “It is a serious wave which breaks best on a HUGE SW swell.”
  - S1 (Wikipedia): “Swell direction: WSW”
- **Acceptable range**: No excerpt states a range of working swell directions.
- **Blocked directions**: No excerpt names swell directions that are blocked or shadowed by land or reefs.
- **Exposure**: Surf-Forecast calls it an exposed reef break with quite reliable surf, and The Inertia says swells come out of the deep Southern Ocean and explode onto the reef.
  - S2 (Surf-Forecast.com): “Shipstern Bluff on the East Coast is an exposed reef break that has quite reliable surf.”
  - S5 (The Inertia): “Out of the deep Southern Ocean, swells explode onto the reef, mutating into heaving right-hand barrels with infamous 'steps' that surfers must navigate”

| Field | Research value | Status | Sources | App model setting |
|---|---|---|---|---|

Notes:

- **Break type**: Surf-Forecast calls it an exposed reef break, The Inertia describes heaving right-hand barrels and Surfer Today (search summary) says the deep-to-shallow reef makes waves that are called slabs.
  - S2 (Surf-Forecast.com): “Shipstern Bluff on the East Coast is an exposed reef break that has quite reliable surf.”
  - S5 (The Inertia): “Out of the deep Southern Ocean, swells explode onto the reef, mutating into heaving right-hand barrels with infamous 'steps' that surfers must navigate”
  - S4 (Surfer Today): “in places with extreme deep-to-shallow reef breaks, such as Tasmania's Shipstern Bluff, the double-up effect becomes so intense that these waves are often referred to as "slabs."”
- **Orientation**: No excerpt states which way the coast or the break faces.
- **Exposure**: Surf-Forecast calls it an exposed reef break.
  - S2 (Surf-Forecast.com): “Shipstern Bluff on the East Coast is an exposed reef break that has quite reliable surf.”
- **Bathymetry**: Surf Atlas says it begins on a shelf of very sharp rock reef, The Age that waves hit a shallow ledge, Surfer Today (search summary) that it is an extreme deep-to-shallow reef and that the reef shape makes a wave within a wave, The Age and WannaSurf describe massive or truck-sized boulders on the floor and in front of the face, and Wikipedia, Surf Atlas, ABC News and The Age describe the resulting steps; no survey is cited.
  - S9 (Surf Atlas (thesurfatlas.com)): “It all begins on a shelf of very sharp rock reef, where huge drifts of water suck back and regularly form 20-30 foot walls.”
  - S8 (The Age): “In the blink of an eye, the waves hit the shallow ledge and transform from a lump in the ocean into a 20-foot (six-metre) face”
  - S4 (Surfer Today): “in places with extreme deep-to-shallow reef breaks, such as Tasmania's Shipstern Bluff, the double-up effect becomes so intense that these waves are often referred to as "slabs."”
  - S8 (The Age): “freefall in a diving position onto the massive boulders on the ocean floor”
  - S6 (WannaSurf): “the very close truck sized boulders in front of the wave face”
  - S3 (Surfer Today): “It is described as a mutant wave that creates a wave within a wave due to the shape of the reef bottom.”
  - S1 (Wikipedia): “The wave is also well known for its multifaceted inner formations, referred to by many of its surfers as steps”
  - S9 (Surf Atlas (thesurfatlas.com)): “Shippies is known for its unpredictable and brutal double ups. The locals call them The Steps, and they are sometimes simply unmakeable.”
  - S7 (ABC News (Australia)): “You get like staircases in the wave and when you ride it you actually have to drop down them”
  - S8 (The Age): “It was like being on a set of stairs, and then suddenly the stairs go straight down and you freefall”

## Conflicting information

- **Swell direction · ideal bearing**: Surf-Forecast gives south southwest (202.5 deg) as the best swell direction, WannaSurf says it breaks best on a huge SW swell (225 deg) and Wikipedia lists WSW (247.5 deg), so the three best directions span 45 deg.
- **Tide · preferred stage**: Wikipedia gives medium to high tide as favourable, while Surf-Forecast says it is best around high tide; both include high tide, but only Wikipedia includes mid tide.
